question: Albania has very serious structural problems concerning transparency, mismanagement and political interference in institutions. The OLAF report for 2023 confirmed the misuse of European funds under IPARD II, as EUR 33 million were classified as unlawfully spent, resulting in Albania being excluded from IPARD III.

At the same time, the 2025 parliamentary elections, although theoretically free, were again characterised by misuse of public funds, unequal campaign conditions and systematic nonimplementation of key OSCE/ODIHR recommendations, in particular regarding the independence and pluralism of the media.
Judicial reforms continue to be undermined by political interference by the Rama regime, serious shortages of effective legal staff and the repeated failure to enforce Constitutional Court decisions.

Of particular concern are recent allegations of selective and surprise demolitions of private properties, including cases with valid permits, without prior judicial protection, as a continuation of an earlier Albanian practice against the homes and churches of the Greek ethnic minority of Northern Epirus.
Such practices directly call into question the separation of powers and respect for property rights and effective access to justice. Accordingly: 1.
How does the Commission justify continuing the accession process without strict and measurable conditionality, when repeated violations of fundamental European principles have been observed?

What concrete and binding measures will the Commission take to ensure that financing, electoral processes and property protection in Albania are linked to real consequences and not mere recommendations?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) The pace of progress in the accession process is based on the fundamentals cluster. The Commission is closely monitoring Albania’s progress in the areas of rule of law, fundamental rights, democracy, and anti-corruption measures. One obligation under the cluster requires the presentation of a roadmap on the functioning of democratic institutions.

As stated in the Commission’s Progress Report on Albania 20251, Albania’s legal framework sets out a generally good basis for the protection of fundamental rights. The adoption in 2025 of a new law on personal data protection, as well as the adoption of implementing legislation on the rights to persons belonging to national minorities represented significant achievements.

As part of the EU integration process, the Commission will continue to support the consolidation of the rule of law and judicial independence in Albania and discuss with the Albanian authorities the proper alignment with the relevant European standards in this area.

The EU closely followed the 2025 parliamentary elections in Albania, including the preliminary findings of the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) of the Organisation for Security Cooperation in Europe.

The Commission will continue to monitor developments in Albania’s democratic institutions, including the adoption of further electoral reforms addressing all ODIHR's key recommendations, also those that are still outstanding from previous elections.

Building on the assistance provided thus far, for example by supporting campaign finance transparency tools and the role of civil society organisations in monitoring the electoral process, targeted technical assistance will continue as relevant, notably to the Central Elections Committee.
Furthermore, the Commission is also monitoring progress in the field of property rights, which is part of the fundamentals cluster.
